answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely from Marcus Aurelius’ ‘Meditations’ (Book 5, section 20). The exact wording here is Gregory Hays’ 2002 translation ↗ — Marcus wrote in Greek, and older renderings (George Long, 1862) are far less pithy: “that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.” The thought is his; this crisp phrasing is the translator’s.

source.excerpt: The mind adapts and converts to its own purposes the obstacle to our acting. The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
trail: The line is section 20 of Book 5 of Marcus Aurelius’ ‘Meditations’ — the George Long public-domain text renders it as “that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road ↗.”
The now-famous crisp wording — “The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way” — comes from Gregory Hays’ 2002 Modern Library translation ↗.
It went viral partly through Ryan Holiday, whose 2014 book ‘The Obstacle Is the Way’ ↗ takes its title directly from this passage.
source.excerptNote: Gregory Hays’ 2002 translation of Meditations 5.20. For comparison, George Long’s 1862 public-domain version reads: “the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid … that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.”

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, the Meditations, was written in Greek during his military campaigns and never intended for publication — a working manual of Stoic self-discipline. This line, from Book 5, distils his conviction that obstacles are raw material for right action, not reasons to stop.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Marcus Aurelius is correct — but people routinely present this exact wording as his own words. It isn’t: he wrote in Greek, and this crisp English phrasing is a modern translator’s.

items.why: The memorable, aphoristic phrasing — “The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way” — is Gregory Hays’ 2002 translation ↗. Marcus’ Greek, in George Long’s 1862 version, reads “that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road ↗” — the same idea, nothing like as quotable.

Much of the line’s modern fame comes via Ryan Holiday’s 2014 bestseller ‘The Obstacle Is the Way’ ↗, whose title is drawn from this passage — so it is frequently quoted as motivational shorthand rather than cited to Book 5.

misattribution.truthLine: Real Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 5.20 ↗) — but the unforgettable wording is Gregory Hays’ 2002 translation, not the emperor’s own words.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Book 5, section 20 sits in a passage about dealing with difficult people. Marcus argues that although others can obstruct our actions, they cannot touch our intentions or dispositions — because the reasoning mind can turn any hindrance into the next thing to work on.

The thought is quintessentially Stoic: externals are “indifferent,” and virtue lies in how we respond. Hays’ 2002 rendering compressed that idea into two hammer-blow sentences, which is why this passage — and not the wordier 19th-century versions — became a modern motto.
